title: Two-year block reordering gave no clear precipitation recovery excess across 344 US divisions in 1901-2020
abstract: We tested whether a reported precipitation recovery excess remains when the reference retains two-year rainfall sequences. We used NOAA nClimDiv monthly precipitation for 344 US divisions in 1901-2020. A low event starts at the calendar-month 10th percentile of a 12-month sum after a median reset. Recovery ends at the median and has a 24-month cap. The observed equal-division mean was 14.162 months from 6,900 episodes. We reordered complete two-year national blocks within five 24-year periods and fit thresholds again in each draw. For 999 draws, the reference mean was 13.998 months, with a central 95% range of 13.640-14.360. The observed excess was 0.164 months and the upper-tail fraction was 0.179. Checks retained separate months and blocks of one, three, four and six years. These are conditional sequence tests. They do not measure water-store recovery or identify a physical memory time. A revised source, fixed block boundaries, within-period exchangeability and the recovery cap limit inference. The package gives code, exact maps, aggregate results, provenance, an arithmetic audit and a figure. Source records remain external.

display.caption: Observed capped recovery mean and six reference distributions. Lines give central 95% reference ranges, not confidence limits. Each reference uses 999 draws. Two-year blocks are the primary test.

citations.reason: We reuse its endpoint code and test the recovery excess under references that retain multiple years. Source records overlap, but the release and tested period differ.
